name: Guerrero Mixteco, dialect of Metlatonoc
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 2 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Overholt, Edward. 1961. The tonemic system of Guerrero Mixteco. In Benjamin F. Elson & Juan Comas (eds.), A William Cameron Townsend en el vigésimoquinto aniversario del Instituto Lingüístico de Verano, 597-626. México: Instituto Lingüístico de Verano.
catalog_locator: pp. 597-598 (opening paragraph and 'Structure-Function' section) and p. 601 (section 'Tone on Voiced Consonants')
catalog_quote: The tonemic system is an especially important part of the dialect spoken in and around the municipality of Metlatonoc, Guerrero, where the data here presented were collected. Tone is, for example, important in this dialect lexically as the distinguishing feature between otherwise homophonous forms. It is important morphologically as the contrastive feature between different aspects of the verb. It is important phonologically because it furnishes criteria for the placement of stress. ... It is tone structure that is the chief differentiating feature between the various aspects of the verb: kātā will weigh (potential), kátā weighing (continuative), kàtā weighed (completive) ... Within an effective verbal context (a stress group or series of them joined into a high-layered unit) voiced consonants carry the tone from one modulation to the next.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: The language is a three-tone language; stress exists and its placement is said to be determined by tonal criteria, and a 'stress group' is a prosodic domain above the morpheme, but the source never states which syllable of the (disyllabic couplet) word carries stress. No placement rule is recoverable from any opened source for metl1238.
new_statements.domain_note: Overholt's unit is the 'morpheme pattern tone unit' (MPTU), basically the disyllabic couplet (CVCV, CVV, CVʔCV, CVʔV; derived CV and CVVV); 'stress group' is mentioned as a phrase-level unit. Data from Metlatónoc and San Rafael, Guerrero (idiolect of Esther López and three other speakers).
new_statements.identity_note: Overholt 1961 (data from Metlatónoc and San Rafael, Metlatónoc municipality) and Martínez Sánchez 2009 (Rancho Nuevo de la Democracia and Metlatónoc) both describe metl1238 proper. The only explicit stress-placement statement found in the group is Zylstra 1980 for Alacatlatzala Mixtec [mim], Glottolog alac1244 (Malinaltepec municipality), a separate language-level languoid under Guerrero Mixtec (guer1245); it is not a statement about metl1238. Glottolog's alternate-name list for metl1238 (Alacatlatzala, Alcozauca, Xochapa, Yoloxóchitl, Guerrero Mixtec) is inherited from ELCat's lumped 'Guerrero Mixtec' entry (10530) and does not make those varieties part of metl1238.

tone_statements.citation: Hillman, George (comp.) & Abraham Rivera (narr.). 1989. Cómo apareció el nombre del pueblo "Cabeza de tigrillo" (Cómo ocurrió la denominación de Quetzalapa). Tlalocan 11: 217-224. México: UNAM, Instituto de Investigaciones Filológicas. doi:10.19130/iifl.tlalocan.1989.126
tone_statements.quote: Cabe mencionar que la palabra catya "tirar" es homófono con caty8 "escarbar", los dos llevando el tono de medio-medio. En el cuento, sólo se diferencian por el efecto que hace al clítico que sigue. Es decir, que catya "escarbar" perturba al clitico que le sigue, meo, de tono bajo a tono alto: yó, mientras que cuya "tirar" no lo perturba; por lo tanto, yQ se queda en tono bajo. Sólo así se distinguen estas dos palabras. [text layer sic: the Mixtec forms 'caty8', 'meo', 'yQ', 'cuya' are scanned-garbled renderings of the printed Mixtec words; Spanish prose verbatim] ... [p. 218 key:] = tono alto / = tono bajo / (sin marca) = tono medio [accent diacritics lost in text layer]
tone_statements.translation: It should be mentioned that the word catya 'throw away' is homophonous with catya 'dig', both carrying the mid-mid tone. In the story they are distinguished only by the effect on the following clitic: catya 'dig' perturbs the clitic that follows it from low tone to high tone, whereas catya 'throw away' does not perturb it, so it stays low. Only thus are these two words distinguished. ... [key:] (acute) = high tone / (grave) = low tone / (unmarked) = mid tone

sources.note: A two-text edition whose introduction gives a first-hand tone note by the SIL fieldworker: two verbs 'tirar' and 'escarbar' are homophonous, both carrying the tone pattern medio-medio, and are distinguished only by sandhi - 'escarbar' perturbs the following low-tone clitic to high tone while 'tirar' leaves it low; the abbreviation key (p. 218) marks three tones: tono alto, tono bajo, '(sin marca) = tono medio'. Confirms a three-level (high/mid/low) lexical tone system with tone perturbation for San Rafael Metlatonoc Mixtec, independent of and 25 years after Overholt 1961.

sources.locator: p. 32, section 1.3 'Proto-Mixtec Tone Sandhi'; also p. 28 dialect area A and p. 37 source list '12 Metlatonoc Met : Overholt 1961 '
sources.note: Reconstructs four Proto-Mixtec tonemic couplets (*HH, *HL, *LL, *LH) plus final glottal stop; gives Metlatónoc reflexes per couplet in terms of Overholt's high/mid/low levels (e.g. *LL > mid-low(-mid), *HL > mid-mid(-low), *HH'/LL' with final high or rising tone), classes Metlatónoc in dialect area A, and states that Metlatónoc morphemes from Proto-Mixtec glottal-final forms cause regular sandhi to high while mid-mid(-low) < *HL causes sandhi to low. Consistent with the 3-level system listed here; adds the diachronic account of Overholt's perturbation classes.
